subject: history
title: Apartheid in South Africa 1948-1994
welcome_lead: Trace the rise, resistance and dismantling of apartheid from the National Party victory in 1948 to Mandela's presidency in 1994.
meta_desc: History Rights & Protest Adventure 2: apartheid laws, resistance and the transition to democracy.
final_note: You have studied the struggle that ended legalised racial separation. The work of redress continues.

walkthroughs.body_html: Building on earlier segregation, the National Party from 1948 enacted laws separating South Africans by race: Population Registration Act, Group Areas Act, Bantu Education Act, Pass Laws and 'separate amenities'. Africans were assigned to ethnic 'homelands' or Bantustans and stripped of South African citizenship in the so-called independent homelands.

The Defiance Campaign (1952), the Freedom Charter (1955), the Sharpeville massacre (1960) and the banning of the ANC and PAC led to the formation of Umkhonto we Sizwe. Mandela's imprisonment (1962-1990), the Soweto Uprising (1976) and the death of Steve Biko (1977) hardened internal and external resistance, including the global anti-apartheid movement and sanctions.

President F. W. de Klerk unbanned political organisations and released Nelson Mandela on 11 February 1990. Negotiations at CODESA, despite serious violence, culminated in non-racial elections on 27 April 1994 won by the ANC. Mandela became South Africa's first democratically elected president; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission followed.
